name: A model that flags risky pull requests is tested on ten PRs that were not used in learning. It calls 4 of them risky, and 3 of those really had a bug; in total 5 of the ten PRs had a bug. Compute and explain its accuracy, precision and recall. Under which three conditions does the score on a test set say how the model will do on new data?
answer: The model was tested on ten pull requests not used in learning, with known outcomes. It was right on 7 of 10: accuracy 70 % – the average of the verdicts (right = 1, wrong = 0). The errors were of two kinds: one false alarm and two missed bugs. Precision: of the 4 PRs it called risky, 3 had a bug – 75 %. Recall: of the 5 PRs with a bug, it found 3 – 60 %. The average says how the model will do on new data only if: (1) the test set is kept apart from learning (being right on a training row after fitting it shows nothing); (2) the known outcomes are right; (3) the test set is like the data we care about – usually a random split of one collection, so for pull requests of another project the 70 % may not hold. Every benchmark can be described with the same boxes: input, model (in its harness), output, reference, grader (program or person) giving a verdict, and the score as the average of verdicts.
keyPoints: Accuracy = share of right verdicts (7/10 = 70 %)
Precision = correct among predicted risky (3/4); recall = found among actual bugs (3/5)
Two error types: false alarms, missed bugs
Conditions: test set separate, labels correct, test set representative
Process: input → model+harness → output vs reference → grader → score

name: What is a classical ML benchmark and why is building one hard? Use the ImageNet challenge as an example.
answer: A benchmark is a published data set with labels, already split into a training and a test set; everybody trains on the same training set and reports the score on the same test set, so models from different teams can be compared on a leaderboard. The three conditions become assumptions about one shared test set (it played no role in building the model, its labels are correct, it looks like the data you care about). Building one is expensive: for the ImageNet challenge (1,000 classes, 1.28 M training images) candidate images came from image search engines queried in five languages, then Amazon Mechanical Turk workers marked which images showed the class; since single workers make mistakes, several workers judged every image and it was kept only with a convincing majority. The test labels were not published; the organisers checked 1,500 by hand and found 5 wrong. Even researchers labelling test images with five guesses were wrong on 13–15 %, and Karpathy reached 5.1 % after training on 500 images. Because this is so much work, a test set is built once and then used for about a decade.
keyPoints: Shared split, published; leaderboard enables comparison
Assumptions: unseen, correctly labelled, representative test set
ImageNet: search engines, MTurk labelling with majority votes
Hidden test labels; hand-check found ~0.3 % errors
Expensive → built once, reused for years

name: Describe the experiment of Recht et al. that built new test sets for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. What was expected, what was found, and what is the lesson?
answer: For years every paper reported on the same test set and models were kept if they scored better on it – adaptive overfitting to the test set was suspected. Recht et al. repeated the original data collection to get new test images (2,000 for CIFAR-10; 10,000 for ImageNet, from similar years, labelled by MTurk workers as originally) and tested the old models. Every model dropped: 3–15 points on CIFAR-10 and 11–14 on ImageNet (e.g. ResNet-152 from 78.3 % to 67.0 %). If overfitting to the test set were the cause, the newest, most tuned models should lose most – but all models lost a similar amount and “the relative order of models is almost exactly preserved”. The authors conclude the drops are caused not by adaptivity but by the models’ inability to generalise to slightly harder images than in the original test sets. Lesson: a benchmark score is a property of the model and of one particular test set; the preserved ranking held for these image classifiers, which is not a general rule.
keyPoints: Hypothesis: adaptive overfitting to a reused test set
New test images collected the same way; old models re-tested
All models dropped (CIFAR-10 3–15, ImageNet 11–14 points)
Ranking preserved → not adaptivity, but poor generalisation to slightly harder images
Score belongs to model + test set; ranking stability not guaranteed elsewhere

name: How common are label errors in widely used test sets, how were they measured, and why do they matter?
answer: Northcutt et al. (NeurIPS 2021) searched ten widely used test sets. A trained classifier predicted a class for every test item, and items where it was confident of a different class than the given label were flagged; five Mechanical Turk workers then saw each flagged item, and it counted as an error if fewer than three agreed with the given label. Only flagged items were checked, so the numbers are lower bounds. In the five image test sets shown in the lecture: MNIST 0.15 %, CIFAR-10 0.54 %, CIFAR-100 5.85 %, ImageNet validation 5.83 %, QuickDraw about 10 %. Why it matters: a model that is right gets marked wrong and a model that learned the mistake gets marked right; rankings can change (on ImageNet with corrected labels, ResNet-18 outperforms ResNet-50 if the share of originally mislabelled test examples rises by just 6 %); and two models that differ by less than the label error rate cannot be reliably told apart by the benchmark.
keyPoints: Classifier flags confident disagreements; 5 MTurk workers verify
Counts are lower bounds
Even MNIST (0.15 %) has errors; ImageNet validation ~5.8 %
Right models penalised, mistaken ones rewarded; rankings can flip
Differences below the error rate are not meaningful

name: Explain benchmark saturation and Goodhart’s law, with examples from image benchmarks.
answer: Saturation: a benchmark gets “solved” and stops separating models. On the ImageNet challenge the winner’s error fell from 28.2 % (2010) to 2.3 % (2017), passing a trained person’s 5.1 % in 2015. MNIST took 14 years to reach near-human performance; ImageNet five; newer data sets now reach that milestone within a few years. Solving the benchmark does not mean the task is solved. Goodhart’s law (usually quoted as “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”; originally about monetary policy) says that a score tells you something about ability only as long as nobody works on the score itself; once models are selected, tuned and advertised by it, it says less. Examples: models chosen by their score on one reused test set; a Baidu team in 2015 made about 200 submissions in half a year to the ImageNet test server (allowed: two per week) and was asked to stay away for a year; gains of tenths of a point reported on benchmarks that no longer separate models.
keyPoints: ImageNet winner error 28.2 % → 2.3 %; beat 5.1 % human in 2015
Time to human level shrinks (MNIST 14 years, ImageNet 5)
Solved benchmark ≠ solved task
Goodhart: measure as target loses meaning
Examples: test-set selection, Baidu’s excess submissions, tiny gains

name: Describe how the MMLU and SWE-bench benchmarks work in terms of input, output, reference, grader and score.
answer: MMLU (2020) is an exam with four options per question: 14,079 test questions from 57 subjects, collected by students from practice exams online. Input: a question with four options; output: text from which a letter A–D is read; reference: the letter of the right option; grader: are the letters equal; score: share of right answers (GPT-3 43.9 %, guessing 25 %). SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., ICLR 2024) uses real GitHub issues: from about 90,000 pull requests in 12 popular Python repositories, scripts kept merged PRs that close an issue and change tests, and tasks that install and run with a test failing before and passing after the fix – 2,294 tasks. Input: the issue and the repository before the fix; output: a patch, usually written by an agent with tools; reference: the tests from the real fix – FAIL_TO_PASS (fail before, must pass) and PASS_TO_PASS (must keep passing); only the test files changed by the fix are run; grader: apply the patch and run the tests, resolved if all pass; score: share of tasks resolved (best model in Oct 2023: 1.96 %). The model sees neither the tests nor the fix. Variants: Lite (300) and Verified (500 human-filtered tasks, 46 % from Django).
keyPoints: MMLU: 4-option questions, letter compared to key, share correct
SWE-bench: issue + repo in, patch out
Reference = hidden tests: FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS
Resolved = all those tests pass; only changed test files run
Collected by scripts (2,294 tasks); Lite 300, Verified 500

name: How can a benchmark’s input be compromised for LLMs? Discuss contamination (the model has seen the items) and solutions leaked in the input, with evidence from MMLU and SWE-bench.
answer: LLMs are trained on web text, and benchmarks are public together with their references. MMLU: Deng et al. hid one wrong option and asked the model to fill it in; ChatGPT reproduced the hidden option exactly in 52 % of cases and GPT-4 in 57 % – knowing wrong options word for word is strong evidence the model has read the test. SWE-bench: the same agent and model (OpenHands with Claude 3.7 Sonnet) solved 43.2 % of Verified but only 19.25 % of 1,319 new issues created since 2024 from 93 repositories (with the caveat that these are also different, unfiltered issues). Given only the issue text and repository name, models named the file to fix in up to 76 % of Verified tasks vs up to 53 % for other repositories – part of a Verified score is memory of twelve well-known code bases, and nobody knows how large a part. Separately, some tasks contain the solution in the issue itself (e.g. sympy #16669, where solving means copying three lines); one preprint found this in 32.67 % of tasks an early agent solved. Also, MNIST measures exactly its task, but LLM benchmarks have names much wider than their items: “75 % of SWE-bench Verified” means resolving 375 mostly small issues in twelve Python libraries.
keyPoints: Public benchmarks + web training → contamination
MMLU: hidden wrong options recited (52 % / 57 %)
SWE-bench: 43.2 % on Verified vs 19.25 % on new issues; file naming without code
Solution sometimes written in the issue
Benchmark names are wider than what the items measure

name: Show with examples that a benchmark score depends not only on the model but also on how the test is run (prompt format, harness, environment).
answer: MMLU format: Alzahrani et al. changed only how the same questions were asked of 11 open models – the order of options, their symbols (e.g. $ & # @ instead of A B C D) and how the model’s choice is determined (most probable letter vs most probable answer text). Models moved by up to 8 places in the ranking; shuffling alone moved them up to 5 (measured on three subjects). One reason: models prefer certain option letters. Unlike ImageNet, the ranking did not survive another way of asking the same questions. Harness: on SWE-bench Verified the same model (Claude 4 Sonnet) solved 64.9 % in bash-only mini-SWE-agent, 66.6 % in SWE-agent and 70.4 % in OpenHands – 5.5 points from the harness alone. So a leaderboard entry is a model in a harness; entries with different harnesses do not compare models. Environment: an agent ran git log --all inside the evaluation container, which still contained later commits, and could find the actual fix (issue #465; history was then removed). And the grader read printed test output, so a patch printing “PASSED <test name>” could count as solved – it is not known that a ranked model did this; the grader now also checks the exit code, though a way around that check has already been reported. The agent is rewarded for “tests pass”; solving the issue must be the only way to get there.
keyPoints: MMLU: option order/symbols/selection method → up to 8 ranking places
Models prefer certain letters
Same model, three harnesses: 64.9 / 66.6 / 70.4 %
Environment loopholes: an agent read future git history; the grader could be fooled by printed PASSED output
Compare models only within one harness and setup

name: What can go wrong with the reference (answer key or tests) of a benchmark? Discuss MMLU errors, tests that are too strict and tests that are too weak in SWE-bench.
answer: MMLU: people re-checked 5,700 questions and estimated that 6.49 % of all MMLU questions contain an error (Virology: 57 %) – unclear questions or options, no correct option, several correct options, or a wrong key (e.g. −47 = g + 24 keyed as −23 instead of −71). On corrected questions the model ranking changes. The cause: the key was copied from websites and never verified item by item. Too strict tests (SWE-bench): in scikit-learn #14501 the issue only asks whether an unused copy parameter is missing something, but the hidden test requires a DeprecationWarning with an exact message decided later by maintainers – other reasonable fixes fail. When building Verified, 93 developers reviewed 1,699 tasks: 38.3 % had underspecified issues and 61.1 % tests that may reject a valid solution; 68.3 % were removed (one objection sufficed). “Verified” means filtered, not rewritten. Too weak tests: in seaborn #2992 the hidden test never tries a value missing only in x, so a patch that does not fix the issue passes. Adding tests to 23 Lite tasks showed 170 of 599 previously passing patches were wrong, changing ranks of 18 of 44 agents on Lite and 11 of 45 on Verified; running all repository tests made 7.8 % of “solved” patches fail. Reviewers of Verified looked only for too strict tests, not too weak ones.
keyPoints: MMLU: ~6.49 % erroneous items; unverified web-sourced key
Too strict: hidden test demands one exact solution not in the issue
Verified: 68.3 % of reviewed tasks removed; filtered, not fixed
Too weak: tests miss the issue’s case; 170/599 passing patches wrong
Rankings change with better references

name: “Resolved” on SWE-bench means the tests pass. Would maintainers actually merge such patches? Describe METR’s study and its findings.
answer: METR gave 296 agent patches that pass the SWE-bench tests (from published runs, models of mid-2024 to late 2025, one attempt per task) and 47 original human patches (all merged in reality, as a control) to four active maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx and pytest, who reviewed them as pull requests without being told who wrote them. They would merge about 68 % of the human patches – so a review is not an exact grader either – but only about a third of the agent patches (roughly half the human rate). Reasons for rejection: the patch does not really solve the issue or breaks other code and the tests did not catch it, or the code is poor in style and ignores project conventions, which tests do not check. A stated limit: the agent had one attempt and no feedback, whereas a human usually gets review feedback and tries again. Conclusion: “resolved” means these tests pass, not that a maintainer would take it. (This also shortens METR’s time horizon: for Claude Sonnet 4.5 about 50 minutes with test verdicts vs about 8 minutes with maintainer verdicts.)
keyPoints: 296 test-passing agent patches + 47 human controls, blind review
Human patches ~68 % mergeable; agent patches ~one third
Rejections: not really fixed, breaks other code, poor style/conventions
Limit: one attempt, no feedback
Tests passing ≠ mergeable

name: Why can two reported benchmark scores often not be compared directly? Discuss task subsets, cost, run-to-run variance, multiple attempts (pass@k, pass^k) and confidence ranges.
answer: Which tasks: GPT-5’s “74.9 % on SWE-bench Verified” was measured on 477 of the 500 tasks (those running on OpenAI’s infrastructure); on all 500 it would lie between 71.4 % and 76.0 %, so it cannot be put next to a 500-task number. Cost: five models in one harness on the same 50 tasks cost between $5 and $1,351, the most expensive run was not the best, and the same score was reached for $403 and $1,331 – a score does not say what was spent. Variance: output is sampled, so each run is one draw; 10 runs of the same setting differed by 2.2–6.0 points, even at temperature 0 (computation is not exactly repeatable). Attempts: Devstral 2 on 500 tasks scores 63.5 % with one attempt (pass@1), 76.2 % if at least one of 5 attempts passes (pass@5 – a best case that needs someone to know which attempt is right), and 49.1 % if all 5 must pass (pass^5 – reliability). Range: with 500 tasks, 75 % has a 95 % range of about ±3.8 points (71.2–78.8 %), so 75 % vs 77 % cannot be ranked from two numbers alone. Yet only 16 % of 445 LLM benchmark papers report any uncertainty estimate.
keyPoints: Subset reporting (477 vs 500 tasks)
Same tasks cost $5–$1,351 (~300×); the same score cost $403 or $1,331
Run-to-run spread 2–6 points, even at T = 0
pass@1 vs pass@k (best case) vs pass^k (reliability)
Confidence range ±3.8 points on 500 tasks; few papers report uncertainty

name: What is METR’s time horizon of a model, how is it measured, what trend does it show, and what are its limits?
answer: METR measures not the share of solved tasks but how long a task an agent can do, in human time. It uses 170 tasks (software engineering, ML, security) that professionals also did; a task’s human time is the typical time of the professionals who solved it, from seconds to hours. A model is run on all tasks, a curve of success probability against human task time is fitted, and the 50 % time horizon is where it crosses 50 % (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Feb 2025: about 1 hour). It is the people’s time, not how long the model worked. The trend: the horizon doubled about every 7 months (207 days), faster for models since 2023 (131 days) – from seconds (GPT-2) to hours (GPT-5 3.6 h, Claude Opus 4.5 5.3 h). Limits: tasks are standalone with automatic checks, unlike real work; the human times are of people new to the code (maintainers were 5–18× faster); “solved” comes from a program – with maintainer verdicts the horizon of Claude Sonnet 4.5 shrank from about 50 to about 8 minutes; at 80 % success the horizon is 4–6× shorter; and ranges are wide (Opus 4.5: 5.3 h, 95 % range 2.8–12 h); METR itself calls measurements above 16 h unreliable.
keyPoints: Tasks timed by human professionals; 50 % success point = horizon
Human time, not model working time
Doubling ~every 7 months (faster recently)
Limits: standalone auto-checked tasks; newcomer human times; test-based verdicts
80 % horizon much shorter; wide confidence ranges

name: You are shown a benchmark number for a model. Summarise how each box of the testing process can fail, and what you should do before trusting the number.
answer: Every box can fail. Input: the model may have seen the items (hidden MMLU options recited; 43 % vs 19 % on new SWE-bench issues). Model + harness: another harness moves the same model by 5.5 points. Output: it is sampled; ten runs differ by 2–6 points. Reference: 6.49 % of MMLU questions are wrong; SWE-bench tests are too strict or too weak (68.3 % of tasks removed for Verified). Grader: tests passing is not correct – maintainers would merge about a third of such patches. Score: ±3.8 points on 500 tasks; 49, 64 or 76 % depending on how attempts are counted; $5 to $1,351 for the same tasks. On top, Goodhart’s law. What to do: (1) read the note under the number – which tasks, harness, attempts, runs, cost, who ran it; (2) open the tasks and check the source (a blog post is a hint until checked); (3) compare with the range – a 1–2 point lead on 500 tasks is a tie; (4) do not overcorrect – large changes (1.96 % → over 75 % on SWE-bench; seconds → hours horizon) are real; (5) measure on your own work – 10–20 tasks from your repository, in your harness, checked by your tests and review (only large differences show, about ±20 points, but they are your tasks). Trust a number as far as you can trace it to its tasks, harness and grader.
keyPoints: Input contamination; harness effects; sampled output
Wrong references; tests ≠ correctness; uncertain, attempt- and cost-dependent scores
Read the note; open the tasks; compare ranges
Don’t overcorrect – big trends are real
Measure on your own tasks, harness and review
